transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-25
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Chris Patel (Zenith Lead Eng), Dana Lopez (Zenith Security), Omar Singh (Zenith PM)

Summary:
Quick walkthrough of Redwood SDKs (Python and TypeScript), auth patterns (API keys, service accounts, SSO), environment setup and quickstarts. Discussed pilot scope, security questions (KMS, audit logs, data retention), and next steps for a dedicated performance pilot.

Topics:
- SDK install and quickstart (pip/npm)
- Auth options and best practices (.env, secrets managers, KMS)
- Example Python and TypeScript snippets for streaming and non-streaming calls
- Console usage for keys, routes, and Optimize recommendations
- Pilot scoping: latency/cost targets, dataset for benchmarks

Action items (captured in metadata above)

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining from Redwood, i'm Alex, i'll kick us off. maya is here from the se team. 
[00:18] Maya: hi all, glad to be here. quick note i might share my screen to run through the quickstart repo and then we can jump into auth and pilot details. 
[00:32] Chris: great, thanks. we just want to see how fast we can get to a PoC, our infra is mostly node + typescript with a small python batch job for offline embeddings.
[00:48] Alex: perfect — that's the typical setup we see. today's demo will show both the TypeScript and Python SDKs, env var patterns, and a short example of streaming generation from the hosted api.
[01:05] Omar: timeline wise we want a pilot in about two weeks, production decisions after the pilot. also security will need SOC2 evidence and KMS support.
[01:22] Dana: yes, we'll need details on key rotation and audit logging; also any VPC/private deployment options because some of our ops are sensitive.
[01:38] Maya: we support three deployment modes — hosted api, dedicated reserved capacity, and private (vpc/on-prem). for quickstarts we usually start with hosted so you can iterate; dedicated is our next step if you need predictable throughput.
[01:56] Chris: good. can you show the npm and pip commands? and how do we manage api keys across envs?
[02:12] Maya: sure, quickshare — i'll paste the commands into the chat. npm i @redwood/inference, pip install redwood-inference-client, sample .env is REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-xxx; REDWOOD_ENV=prod or staging. we recommend using your cloud secrets manager (aws secrets manager / gcp secret manager) and not checking .env into repo.
[02:40] Alex: also service accounts are supported for private deployments; for hosted we use API keys with role-based scopes you can rotate. we'll show a demo of creating a key in the console.
[02:58] [Maya shares screen: GitHub repo quickstart]
[03:10] Maya: repo structure: /python/quickstart.py, /ts/quickstart.ts, dockerfile, and a simple benchmark script. for python example, quickstart snippet:
[03:35] Speaker 1: import redwood
client = redwood.Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
resp = client.generate('summarize product reviews')
print(resp.text)
[03:56] Maya: note that's a simplified paste from the transcript, actual api includes model param, max_tokens, streaming flag etc.
[04:12] Chris: and for typescript?
[04:20] Maya: ts snippet:
[04:28] Speaker 2: import { Redwood } from '@redwood/inference'
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
const resp = await client.generate({ model: 'redwood-7b', prompt: '...' })
console.log(resp.text)
[04:52] Omar: what's the recommended pattern for streaming in node? web sockets or server-sent events?
[05:00] Maya: we provide both streaming over http (chunked transfer) and a websocket sdk helper. stream example in ts shows client.stream(...). on the server side you can pipe chunks to clients.
[05:18] Dana: how do you handle long conversation context and kv cache across calls? we do multi-turn with long contexts.
[05:28] Maya: runtime keeps a kv cache; for multi-turn you supply conversation id so it can reuse kv. with dedicated you get more control over cache lifetime and pinning. there are occasional mismatch transcriptions — sorry, i said kv cache but the cli name in docs is kv-cache TTL, minor wording.
[05:50] Chris: can we set token limits and cost estimations programmatically?
[05:56] Alex: yes, you can set max_tokens and top_p; console shows token-level cost breakdowns and our optimize tool will recommend quantization/batch sizes based on throughput to lower unit cost.
[06:12] Omar: for the pilot we need to simulate our peak qps, about 400 rps with 7-12 token bursts. any guidance?
[06:23] Maya: that's high but doable with ded- pools. we'll propose an autoscale profile, suggest batching window 10-20ms and a quantized model if latency sensitivity allows. i'll add that to the pilot deck.
[06:39] Chris: security: SSO with SAML? we want role-based access in console for our engineers and separate audit logs for infra.
[06:49] Alex: we support SSO/SAML, fine-grained RBAC, KMS integration for private key management, and audit logs exportable to your SIEM. Dana, we can share SOC2 and ISO docs after the call.
[07:05] Dana: please include specifics on KMS key wrapping and HSM options. also retention policy for logs and customer data.
[07:16] Maya: noted. for data in hosted endpoints we can configure retention and masking; private deployment keeps everything in your network. 
[07:30] [10 min mark summary by Alex] quick re-cap, we'll send quickstart repo, schedule pilot, and share security pack.
[07:50] [08:00] Chris: ok let's dive deeper into the typescript example and error handling.
[08:10] Maya: example for retry/backoff: use the client built-in retry with exponential backoff; sample config: retries:3, backoffMs: 200. for rate limits we recommend client-side token bucket.
[08:28] Speaker 3: (mumbling) also watch out for partial streams — server can send partial tokens, handle incomplete json if you're streaming structured outputs.
[08:45] Maya: good point, we have a helper to assemble streaming json events.
[09:00] Chris: can you show signing requests if we want to proxy through our edge?
[09:08] Maya: yes you can create short-lived session tokens in the console or issue service-account keys. for proxying use the Authorization: Bearer <token> header; we have examples for nginx and envoy in the repo.
[09:26] Omar: what about regional routing? we need EU data residency for some customers.
[09:33] Alex: you can pin region per route in the console; hosted has EU regions and private can be deployed in your VPC in eu-west. for compliance we will document region guarantees.
[09:48] Chris: stream latency — what should we expect 95th p95?
[09:55] Maya: depends on model and region; for redwood-7b in hosted eu region baseline p95 is ~180ms for short prompts, but with high qps and batching you can see variations. dedicated improves consistency — SLOs can be discussed in the pilot.
[10:12] Dana: encryption at rest and in transit? we require both and KMS key control.
[10:18] Alex: we do TLS in transit and encryption at rest; private supports customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM.
[10:28] Chris: can we test both streaming and batch embeddings in the pilot?
[10:34] Maya: absolutely; send your workload sample and we'll run throughput and latency benchmarks and give recommended quantization model variants.
[10:45] [12:00] Alex: quick demo of console — creating an api key (slight audio glitch) — you go to console.redwood.ai -> project -> api keys -> create key -> set scopes.
[12:20] Maya: showing routes tab — you can create per-route model pinning and region pins. optimize tab gives batching and quant recommendations with estimated cost savings.
[12:38] Chris: who typically owns the billing and seat assignments?
[12:45] Alex: enterprise can map to accounts and subteams; billing owner is typically an ops manager, seats managed via SSO group sync.
[12:58] Omar: any gotchas when upgrading SDK versions?
[13:05] Maya: we publish semver and changelogs; breaking changes are flagged and we provide migration guides in repo. for private deployments we coordinate upgrades via the region ticket.
[13:20] Chris: in typescript, do we get types for responses?
[13:24] Maya: yes, the ts sdk exports types and helpers for structured output, plus a typed streaming iterator.
[13:35] Dana: on audit logs, can we push to our splunk?
[13:40] Alex: yes, logs can be exported to your SIEM, we support push and pull mechanisms and webhook sinks.
[13:52] Omar: for the pilot cost, what's a rough estimate for a 2-week benchmark at 400 rps?
[14:00] Maya: we'll need the average token length distribution; rough guesstimate 2 weeks at that qps could be high but we'll provide a committed estimate in the pilot proposal.
[14:12] Chris: ok we'll share token histogram.
[14:18] Maya: also small note, in the repo the rust helper was misnamed — docs say kv-cache TTL but the flag name is cache-ttl, minor doc mismatch.
[14:32] [20 min mark] Alex: let's demo the python quickstart run — maya over to you.
[14:40] Maya: running python quickstart now, pip install redwood-inference-client, export REDWOOD_API_KEY, python quickstart.py
[14:58] [screen shows quickstart output with a few transcription artifacts, 'reponse' instead of response]
[15:10] Maya: seen stray typos in the sample output, ignore that — core flow: client instantiation, generate call, check resp. we also have an embeddings helper for offline batch runs.
[15:25] Chris: show how to swap models for cost/latency tradeoffs programmatically.
[15:33] Maya: set model param to redwood-7b or an 3b quantized variant; use model aliases in console to switch without code changes.
[15:46] Alex: that aliasing is helpful for rollouts — map alias to different model versions and do canary traffic splits.
[15:58] Omar: logging / observability integration? we want per-request token cost breakdown.
[16:05] Maya: the console provides token-level cost and tracing hooks you can forward to your observability stack; we also surface per-route dashboards and sample traces.
[16:20] Dana: can we get a signed mfa requirement for console admin?
[16:26] Alex: yes, we enforce SSO with 2FA and can require hardware keys for admin roles.
[16:34] Chris: any sandbox or free tier for devs?
[16:38] Alex: dev credits and free test keys for small scale, yes.
[16:44] [25 min mark] Maya: quick note on error handling in TS streaming — you'll want to handle event chunks that may not include the final token; the helper library reconstructs partial messages and yields complete events.
[17:00] Chris: ok useful. about the private deployment, do we need to open ports?
[17:06] Maya: for private we install a control plane connector and use customer VPC peering or private link; we provide a checklist for network config.
[17:18] Dana: how do you handle data deletion requests?
[17:24] Alex: we have DSR flow — record request, delete associated data, and provide attestation for hosted customers; private customers manage their own storage.
[17:36] Omar: anything else on data encryption?
[17:40] Maya: envelopes and kms wrapping, you can bring your own keys for private, for hosted we support customer-managed keys for certain enterprise tiers.
[17:52] [30 min mark] Alex: let's outline the pilot: 2 weeks, simulate peak traffic, run streaming + batch embeddings, measure latency p50/p95, and compare hosted vs dedicated.
[18:06] Maya: deliverables: benchmark results, config recommendations (batching, quantization, autoscale), pilot cost estimate.
[18:16] Chris: sounds good. please include a simple checklist for our infra team.
[18:22] Alex: will do.
[18:30] Dana: also include SOC2 control mappings and evidence types we can expect.
[18:36] Alex: will attach security pack; dana, you'll get a dedicated contact.
[18:42] [wrap-up recap by Alex] we'll send the quickstart repo, security docs, pilot proposal and schedule a follow-up sync.
[18:54] Chris: thanks, that works.
[19:00] Omar: thanks everyone.
[19:08] Maya: thanks all, talk soon.
